etymology: Hebrew 'iyyon, “ruin” or “heap,” a fortified town in the far north of the land, in the territory of the tribe of Naphtali.
biblical_def: Ijon was a town in the uttermost north of the land of Israel, within the borders of Naphtali, lying near the upper waters that feed the Jordan. It is named first among the cities that Ben-hadad king of Syria smote when Asa king of Judah hired him to break the league he had with Baasha king of Israel: he “smote Ijon, and Dan, and Abel-beth-maachah” (1Ki 15:20). Long after, when the Assyrian came up, Tiglath-pileser took Ijon among the northern cities and carried their people captive into Assyria (2Ki 15:29). The dictionary does not labour the bare points of its situation; what it honours is that this border town stood among the goodly heritage the LORD measured out to His people, and that even its smiting was not outside His government. The lines were fallen unto Naphtali in pleasant places, and the bounds of their habitation were set by the same God who divided to the nations their inheritance (Deu 32:8; Act 17:26). Ijon’s capture warns that a portion held in unbelief may be plucked away, yet it witnesses also that the God who gave the land governs both its keeping and its loss. No town of the saint’s heritage is too small for the care, or the chastening, of Him who apportioned it.

etymology: Hebrew chuqoq, “appointed” or “decreed,” from a root meaning to engrave or decree, a town on the border of the tribe of Naphtali.
biblical_def: Hukok was a town that marked the border of the inheritance of the tribe of Naphtali in the north of the land. It is named where the boundary of Naphtali turned westward and the coast reached “to Hukok, and reached to Zebulun on the south side, and reached to Asher on the west side” (Jos 19:34). Thus it stood at a point where three tribes met, a quiet landmark by which the LORD’s exact dividing of the land was measured. The dictionary does not labour the obscure points of its situation; what it honours is that the very name of the town bespeaks something decreed and appointed, for the bounds of every tribe were not the work of chance but of the God who divideth to every man severally as He will. The lines were fallen unto Naphtali in pleasant places, and a goodly heritage was theirs (Psa 16:6). He who set the borders of the tribes hath determined the times before appointed and the bounds of His people’s habitation (Deu 32:8; Act 17:26). Hukok stands as a witness that no boundary of the saint’s portion is arbitrary; each is engraven by the appointment of Him who removeth not the ancient landmark of His own faithful dividing, but keepeth it sure.

etymology: Hebrew qanah, “reeds” or “place of reeds,” a town on the border of the tribe of Asher, sharing its name with the brook or river Kanah.
biblical_def: Kanah was a town that lay on the border of the inheritance of the tribe of Asher, named where the coast of Asher reached “unto Kanah, even unto great Zidon” (Jos 19:28). The same name belonged also to a brook, the river Kanah, which ran along the boundary between Ephraim and Manasseh (Jos 16:8); whether the town took its name from a like place of reeds or from such a watercourse, the dictionary does not labour the matter. What it honours is that this border town was numbered among the goodly heritage the LORD measured out to Asher, hard by the great city of Zidon at the edge of the land. The name speaks of reeds, of a humble and watered place, yet the bounds of Asher were set by no chance hand but by the God who divideth to the nations their inheritance and setteth the bounds of His people (Deu 32:8; Act 17:26). The lines were fallen unto Asher in pleasant places (Psa 16:6). Kanah stands as a witness that the LORD knoweth the least landmark of His people’s portion, the very brooks and reed-beds by which their borders ran, and that nothing of the saint’s inheritance is too small or too lowly for the care of Him who apportioned it.

etymology: Hebrew nahalal, “pasture” or “watering place,” a town of the tribe of Zebulun, set apart as a city of the Levites.
biblical_def: Nahalal was a town in the inheritance of the tribe of Zebulun, named among the cities of their allotment in the north of the land (Jos 19:15). When the Levites, who received no portion of land for themselves, were given cities to dwell in throughout the tribes, Nahalal was numbered among the cities of Zebulun granted to the children of Merari for their habitation (Jos 21:35). Yet Scripture records also that Zebulun “did not drive out the inhabitants of Kitron, nor the inhabitants of Nahalol” (Jdg 1:30), so that the Canaanite dwelt among them and became tributaries. The dictionary does not labour the bare points of its situation; what it honours is twofold. First, the name speaks of pasture and a place of watering, a quiet portion in Zebulun’s goodly heritage (Psa 16:6). Second, that this pasture-town was given to the Levites teaches that the LORD Himself was the portion of His ministers; though they held no tribe’s land, He scattered their dwellings among His people that the law might be near to every house. The bounds of Zebulun and the cities of the Levites alike were set by Him who divideth to the nations their inheritance (Deu 32:8). Nahalal stands as a witness that the unfinished obedience of Israel could not undo the faithful apportioning of God.

etymology: Hebrew sarid, “survivor” or “remnant” (that which is left), a town marking the southern border of the tribe of Zebulun.
biblical_def: Sarid was a town that marked the border of the inheritance of the tribe of Zebulun in the north of the land. From it the boundary line was measured: the border of their lot “went up toward the sea, and Maralah, and reached to Dabbasheth, and reached to the river that is before Jokneam” (Jos 19:11), and again “from Sarid eastward toward the sunrising unto the border of Chisloth-tabor” (Jos 19:12). Thus Sarid stood as a fixed landmark from which the men of Israel reckoned the bounds of Zebulun’s goodly heritage. The dictionary does not labour the bare points of its situation; what it honours is that the very name of the town speaks of a remnant, a thing left and surviving, and that the LORD set His people’s borders with a remnant in His eye. The lines were fallen unto Zebulun in pleasant places (Psa 16:6), and the bounds of their habitation were determined by Him who divideth to the nations their inheritance (Deu 32:8; Act 17:26). Sarid stands as a witness that the God who measured this border is the same who hath ever preserved a remnant according to the election of grace, and that no landmark of His faithful dividing is moved without His hand. He removeth not the ancient landmark which the fathers have set (Pro 22:28).

etymology: Hebrew shi'on, “overturning” or “ruin,” a town in the inheritance of the tribe of Issachar in the north of the land.
biblical_def: Shion was a town in the allotment of the tribe of Issachar, named among the cities of their lot in the north of the land (Jos 19:19). It is recorded with Jezreel, Chesulloth, and Shunem as part of the goodly heritage the LORD measured out to Issachar, the tribe of whom Jacob said that he “saw that rest was good, and the land that it was pleasant” (Gen 49:15). The dictionary does not labour the bare points of its situation, for Shion appears but once and is named no more; what it honours is that this all-but-forgotten town was numbered by the LORD among the portions of His people. The lines were fallen unto Issachar in pleasant places, and a goodly heritage was theirs (Psa 16:6). The bounds of their habitation were not the work of chance but of the God who divideth to the nations their inheritance and setteth the bounds of the people according to His own counsel (Deu 32:8; Act 17:26). Shion stands as a witness that the obscurity of a place in the eyes of men is no measure of its standing in the record of God. A town named but once, never to be spoken of again, is yet written for ever in the book of the LORD’s faithful dividing of the land, and so no portion of the saint’s heritage, however hidden, is forgotten by Him who apportioned it.

etymology: Hebrew remeth, “height” or “high place,” a town in the inheritance of the tribe of Issachar in the north of the land.
biblical_def: Remeth was a town in the allotment of the tribe of Issachar, named among the cities of their lot together with En-gannim, En-haddah, and Beth-pazzez (Jos 19:21). Its name speaks of a height or a high place, and like its neighbours it appears but once in the sacred record, a quiet portion of the goodly heritage the LORD measured out to Issachar in the north. The dictionary does not labour the bare points of its situation; what it honours is that this little hill-town was numbered by the LORD among the portions of His people, set down by name in the roll of the inheritance. The lines were fallen unto Issachar in pleasant places (Psa 16:6), and the bounds of their habitation were determined by the God who divideth to the nations their inheritance and setteth the bounds of the people (Deu 32:8; Act 17:26). A height in the eyes of men is a small thing, soon forgotten; but Remeth stands as a witness that the LORD remembereth every landmark of His people’s portion, and that the obscurity of a place is no bar to its place in the faithful record of His dividing. He removeth not the ancient landmark which the fathers have set (Pro 22:28), but keepeth the bounds of the inheritance sure from generation to generation, that His people might dwell in safety in the portion He apportioned.

etymology: Hebrew rabbith, “multitude” or “great” (from a root meaning many or much), a town in the inheritance of the tribe of Issachar in the north of the land.
biblical_def: Rabbith was a town in the allotment of the tribe of Issachar, named among the cities of their lot together with Kishion, Abez, and Remeth (Jos 19:20). Its name speaks of a multitude or of greatness, from a root signifying many or much, though in Scripture it appears but once, never to be named again. The dictionary does not labour the bare points of its situation; what it honours is that this little town, whose very name bespeaks abundance, was numbered by the LORD among the portions of His people in the goodly heritage He measured out to Issachar. The lines were fallen unto Issachar in pleasant places (Psa 16:6), and the bounds of their habitation were set by the God who divideth to the nations their inheritance (Deu 32:8; Act 17:26). There is a fitting lesson in a place called “multitude” that is spoken of but once: the greatness of men’s names is fleeting, but the faithfulness of God in His dividing endureth. Rabbith stands as a witness that the LORD setteth down by name even the towns the world soon forgets, and that no portion of the saint’s heritage, however lightly esteemed among men, is lost from the record of Him who apportioned it and keepeth its bounds sure.

etymology: Hebrew 'eyn chatsor, “spring of Hazor” or “fountain of the enclosure,” a fenced city in the inheritance of the tribe of Naphtali.
biblical_def: En-hazor was a fenced city in the allotment of the tribe of Naphtali, named among the strong cities of their lot together with Kedesh, Edrei, and Iron (Jos 19:37). Its name signifies a spring or fountain of Hazor, joining the Hebrew word for a fountain with the name of an enclosure or settlement, and it is to be distinguished from the great city of Hazor that Joshua burned. The dictionary does not labour the bare points of its situation; what it honours is that this walled town with its spring was numbered by the LORD among the fenced cities of Naphtali’s goodly heritage in the north of the land. The lines were fallen unto Naphtali in pleasant places (Psa 16:6), and the bounds of their habitation, with all their fenced cities and fountains of water, were set by the God who divideth to the nations their inheritance (Deu 32:8; Act 17:26). A city is fenced for safety, and a spring is given for life; in En-hazor both meet, and both bespeak the providence of God toward His people. En-hazor stands as a witness that the LORD who apportioned the land furnished it also for the dwelling of His people, giving them strong cities to keep them and living water to sustain them, that they might dwell safely in the portion His own hand had measured.

etymology: Hebrew 'aphekah, “fortress” or “enclosure” (from a root meaning to be strong or to hold fast), a town in the hill country of the tribe of Judah.
biblical_def: Aphekah was a town in the hill country of the tribe of Judah, named among the cities of their inheritance together with Humtah, Kirjath-arba, and Zior (Jos 15:53). Its name speaks of a fortress or stronghold, from a root signifying strength and holding fast, and it is to be distinguished from the several towns named Aphek that lay elsewhere in the land. The dictionary does not labour the bare points of its situation; what it honours is that this hill-town was numbered by the LORD among the cities of Judah, the tribe of the kingly line out of which the Lion of Judah should come. The lines were fallen unto Judah in pleasant places (Psa 16:6), and the bounds of their habitation were set by the God who divideth to the nations their inheritance (Deu 32:8; Act 17:26). There is a quiet fitness in a stronghold among the cities of Judah, for the LORD Himself is the strong tower of His people, and the name of a little hill-fortress may turn the heart to Him who is the true fortress and high tower of the saints. Aphekah stands as a witness that the LORD who apportioned the hill country of Judah is the same who is the refuge and the strength of all who trust in Him, and that no portion of His people’s heritage lies outside His keeping.
